title: Commercial interests shaping state policy
description: Commercial actors and governments can have overlapping interests; the two cases show different documented channels, not a universal causal rule.

title: Privatized gains, socialized risk
description: British parliamentary intervention followed the East India Company's financial crisis, providing a case for investigating risk allocation and accountability.

title: Covert intervention and long-term blowback
description: The 1953 Iranian coup allows the long-term political consequences of covert intervention to be investigated; specific causal effects remain under review.

title: Imperial fiscal stress, corporate relief and contested legitimacy
description: The same empire faced state debt, colonial taxation disputes and an East India Company financial crisis. Overlapping policies affected different groups differently, without requiring one unified secret plan.

title: Public borrowing backed by charters, taxes, and corporate capital
description: Britain's late seventeenth- and early eighteenth-century rulers financed wartime and other public obligations through subscribed company capital, tax-backed interest, and charters. The Bank, rival East India firms, and South Sea Company had distinct purposes and sometimes competed. The documented arrangement is a repeatable institutional mechanism, not proof that any one family directed centuries of outcomes.

title: Debt-to-equity conversion, political privilege and investment risk
description: South Sea Company debt conversion illustrates how public financing schemes can create market incentives, lobbying contests, investor gains and losses, and political-accountability questions. Financial and parliamentary archives must be consulted before attributing misconduct to named individuals.

title: Debt refinancing, chartered monopolies and colonial promotional narratives
description: French and British governments pursued different but comparable public-debt refinancing models using chartered trading companies, share issues and privileges. Promotional claims about colonial riches circulated alongside coerced labor and Indigenous dispossession. Historical connections across markets are documented, while single-group command is not established.
